claims.text: High configurational entropy slows the diffusion of key reactive elements such as Cr or Al.
Slower diffusion promotes selective segregation of reactive elements to the alloy surface.
Surface segregation of reactive elements produces a thin, uniform, and adherent protective oxide barrier.
The proposed alloy is homogeneous, has a multi-principal-element composition, and contains sufficient Cr or Al to form a protective oxide.
Cr and Al are reactive elements capable of forming protective oxides.
Holding temperature and oxygen partial pressure constant ensures that diffusion processes govern the oxidation behavior.
High configurational entropy induces lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion retards atomic diffusion in the high-entropy alloy.
Retarded atomic diffusion causes selective segregation of reactive elements to the alloy surface.
Suppressed interdiffusion causes key oxide-forming elements to accumulate at the surface.
At high temperature, surface-enriched oxide-forming elements oxidize preferentially.
Preferential oxidation forms a thin, uniform, and adherent protective oxide layer.
The protective oxide layer limits further oxygen ingress.
Relative to a lower-mixing-entropy alloy with similar reactive-element content, the high-entropy alloy will form a thinner, more continuous, and slower-growing oxide scale.
The high-entropy alloy will exhibit lower oxidation mass gain and improved oxide-scale adhesion relative to the baseline.
The proposed mechanism is applicable at approximately 900–1200 °C under controlled oxygen partial pressure when sufficient reactive element is present.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when secondary phases or external stresses dominate oxidation behavior.
The magnitude of diffusion retardation and reactive-element segregation may vary with alloy composition and microstructure.
A controlled comparison uses high-entropy and conventional alloys with similar reactive-element content under identical oxidation conditions.
Failure of the high-entropy alloy to produce a significantly thinner, more uniform, more adherent, and slower-growing scale than the conventional alloy would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The account says that retarding or suppressing diffusion causes oxide-forming elements to segregate and accumulate at the surface, but it does not explain how reduced elemental mobility supplies those elements to the surface. The claimed direction of the diffusion effect is therefore mechanistically in tension with the asserted surface enrichment.
